title: 想 vs 要 in Chinese: HSK 1 Grammar with Examples
description: 想 or 要? How to say "want" in Chinese: would like to, going to, have to, miss someone, negatives, questions, the common mistake, and HSK 1 examples.
h1: 想 vs 要: "Want To", "Would Like To" and "Will"
lede: Both 想 (xiǎng) and 要 (yào) can mean "want", and both go straight before the verb. 想 is softer, like "would like to" or "feel like". 要 is firmer: you have decided, you need to, or it is going to happen.

paras: 想 is for wishes and plans you are thinking about, like "would like to" or "feel like" in English. It is a polite, gentle way to say what you want. You can make it stronger with 很: 我很想去 means "I really want to go".

examples.en: What would you like to eat?
I'd really like to go to China.
I'd like to have a short rest.

sections.h2: 要 + verb: want to, have to, going to
paras: 要 sounds more decided than 想. Depending on the context it can mean "want to", "have to" or "am going to". 我要工作 can be "I have to work" or "I'll be working": either way, it is happening. Unlike 想, 要 does not take 很 in this meaning.

examples.py: Wǒ yào mǎi yì běn shū.
examples.en: I want to buy a book.
I'm going to the hospital tomorrow.

paras: Put 要 before the verb and 了 at the end to say something is going to happen very soon. This is not about wanting at all, so it works for the weather and for things nobody chooses.

examples.en: Our class is about to start.

sections.h2: With a noun: 要 means want, 想 means miss
paras: To ask for a thing, such as food in a restaurant or something in a shop, use 要 + noun, or the softer 想要 + noun.

This is where the most common learner mistake happens. 想 + a person or place means "miss": 我想妈妈了 is "I miss Mum". So 我想米饭 does not mean "I'd like rice"; say 我要米饭 or 我想要米饭 instead. 想 can also mean "think", as in 我想他今天不来了.

examples.py: Wǒ xiǎng yào yí ge xīn shǒujī.
Wǒ xiǎng tā jīntiān bù lái le.
examples.en: I don't think he's coming today.

paras: To say you don't want to do something, use 不想 + verb: 我不想去. Be careful with 不要 + verb: it usually means "don't!", telling someone not to do something. With a noun, 我不要 is fine and simply means "I don't want it".
Ask with 吗 at the end, or with the verb-not-verb pattern: 你想不想……? and 你要不要……? 你要不要 is a very common way to offer something.

examples.en: I want this one, not that one.

examples.py: Nǐ xiǎng bu xiǎng kàn diànyǐng?
examples.en: Do you want to see a film?

examples.py: Nǐ yào bu yào hē shuǐ?
